title: Build Your First Web Page: Gritt-ify
summary: Make a small fan page for Gritty, the orange mascot. You build the page with HTML, then add colour and size with CSS kept in its own file.
outcome: A web page called Gritt-ify with a purple banner, a picture of Gritty, a heading, a sign-up box and a list of posts, all styled with your own CSS file.
learns: Set up project folders and files
Build a page with HTML tags
Show a picture using a file path
Connect a CSS file to a page
Style things using class and id names
Change colours, sizes, spacing and boldness

files.content:
Gritty's landing banner

Cause everything's better with Gritty's face on it.

Gritter

Social media dedicated to Gritty... and only Gritty... cause he's a psycho.

  • Hey there, it's Gritty again.
  • I haven't eaten any other mascots since yesterday.
  • Burp.

steps.title: See what we'll build
steps.instruction: Watch Brendan explain the plan: a fun fan page for Gritty with a banner, a picture and a list of posts.
steps.why: Knowing the goal makes every step easier to follow.
hints: Just watch for now, nothing to type.
Notice the two parts of the page: a banner at the top and a Gritter section below.
When the overview ends, move on to setup.

steps.title: Make a project folder
steps.instruction: Watch Brendan make a folder called DevProject. All the files for this website will live inside one folder like this.
steps.why: Keeping a project in one folder means every file can find the others.
hints: Nothing to type yet.
Watch where the folder gets created.
The folder is named DevProject.

concept.title: Project folders
concept.explain: A website is just a folder of files; keeping them together lets the page find its pictures and styles.

steps.title: Create the files and folders
steps.instruction: Watch Brendan open the folder in VS Code and make: a file called index.html, a folder called resources, inside it a folder called css with a file index.css, and a folder called images. Your project here already has the same layout.
steps.why: A tidy layout makes file paths short and easy to write later.
hints: Just watch how the folders sit inside each other.
index.html is at the top; index.css is inside resources, then css.
The picture will go inside resources, then images.

steps.title: Add Gritty's picture
steps.instruction: Watch Brendan copy a picture called better_than_drake.png into the resources/images folder. Put any picture you like there with that exact name.
steps.why: The page can only show a picture that sits in your project.
hints: Find a picture you want to use.
It goes inside resources, then images.
Name it better_than_drake.png.

steps.title: Start the page
steps.instruction: In index.html, type the first line <!DOCTYPE html>, which tells the browser this is a modern web page. Then add an html tag with lang="en" (the page is in English) and, inside it, an empty head tag. Close both.
steps.why: Every web page starts with this outer shell; the head holds facts about the page.

checks.say: I can't see the outer page wrapper with the English language setting yet.
checks.name: lang

checks.say: Something in your page looks unfinished. Check every tag is closed.

hints: Start with the special first line, then the outer wrapper with the head inside it.
First line is the DOCTYPE. Next an html opening tag with a lang setting, then head opening and closing tags, then close html.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="…">
<head>
…
</html>

concept.title: HTML tags
concept.explain: HTML uses tags in angle brackets, like <head> and </head>, to wrap and label each part of a page.

steps.title: Add page info and a title
steps.instruction: Inside the head, add three meta lines (meta tags give the browser settings, like the letter set and screen size). Then add a title tag with the text Gritt-ify. The title is what shows on the browser tab.
steps.why: These settings help the page look right on every screen, and the title names your tab.
steps.expected:
<meta charset="UTF-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="ie=edge">
    <title>Gritt-ify</title>

checks.say: I can't see a tab title in the top part of your page yet.
Your tab title should say Gritt-ify.
I can't find the letter set setting yet.
checks.name: charset

hints: The head needs some settings and a name for the browser tab.
Between the head opening and closing tags, add three meta tags (charset, viewport, X-UA-Compatible) and then a title tag.

<meta charset="…">
<meta name="viewport" content="…">
<meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="…">
<title>…</title>

concept.title: The head and title
concept.explain: The head holds information about the page; the title is the name shown on the browser tab.

steps.title: Add the body and banner box
steps.instruction: After the closing head tag, add a body tag (everything you can see goes in here). Inside it, write a note <!-- Banner section --> (notes like this are hidden from visitors), then a div with class="banner". A div is a plain box that groups things. Close the div and body.
steps.why: The class name banner lets us colour this box later with CSS.

checks.say: I can't see the banner box on your page yet.

hints: The visible part of the page needs its own section, with a box inside for the banner.
Right after the head closes, open body, write the hidden note, then a div with the class banner, then close div and body.

concept.title: Classes
concept.explain: A class is a name you give a box so you can style it, and you can reuse it many times.

steps.title: Fill the banner
steps.instruction: Inside the banner div, add three lines: an h1 (the biggest heading) saying Gritty's landing banner, a p (a paragraph of text) saying Cause everything's better with Gritty's face on it., and a button saying Subscribe to me or I'll eat you.
steps.why: Headings, text and buttons are the basic pieces of almost every web page.
steps.expected:
Gritty's landing banner

Cause everything's better with Gritty's face on it.

checks.say: I can't see a big heading in the banner yet.
Your heading should mention Gritty.
I can't see the paragraph in the banner yet.
I can't see the button in the banner yet.

hints: The banner needs a heading, a sentence and a button.
Between the div's opening and closing tags, add an h1, then a p, then a button, each with its own text.

…

…

concept.title: Headings, paragraphs, buttons
concept.explain: h1 makes a big heading, p makes a paragraph, and button makes something people can click.

steps.title: Start the Gritter section
steps.instruction: At the end of the body, after the banner, add the note <!-- Gritter section --> and a new div. Inside it put a span (a small piece of text) with id="gritter" saying Gritter, and a paragraph with class="bold" about Gritty's social media. An id is a name only one thing on the page may use.
steps.why: The id and class names let us style these later.
steps.expected:
Gritter

Social media dedicated to Gritty... and only Gritty... cause he's a psycho.

checks.say: I can't see the Gritter title yet.
The Gritter title should say Gritter.
I can't see the paragraph named bold yet.

hints: Make a second box below the banner with a title and a sentence.
After the banner's closing div, add the hidden note, then a div holding a span with the id gritter and a p with the class bold.

…

…

concept.title: IDs
concept.explain: An id is a unique name for one thing on the page, so you can style just that one.

steps.title: Add a post box
steps.instruction: Under the bold paragraph, add a form (a group of boxes people fill in) with action="". Inside, add an input with type="text" (a typing box) and an input with type="submit" and value="Submit" (a send button).
steps.why: Forms let visitors type things into your page.

checks.say: I can't see a typing box yet.
I can't see the Submit button in your form yet.

hints: Add a place where someone could type a post and send it.
Right after the bold paragraph, open a form, add two input tags (one of type text, one of type submit), then close the form.

<form action="">
    <input type="…">
    <input type="…" value="…">
</form>

concept.title: Forms and inputs
concept.explain: A form groups input boxes and buttons so visitors can type and send information.

steps.title: Add the first post
steps.instruction: After the form, add a ul (a bulleted list) with one li (a list item) inside. In the li, put two divs inside each other holding a span that says Hey there, it's Gritty again.
steps.why: Lists are perfect for a feed of posts, one item per post.

checks.say: I can't see the list of posts yet.
Your first post should say Hey there, it's Gritty again.

hints: Make a list with one post in it.
After the form closes, open a ul, inside it an li, inside that two divs and a span with the message, then close everything.
• …

concept.title: Lists
concept.explain: ul makes a bulleted list, and each li inside it is one item in that list.

steps.title: Show Gritty's picture
steps.instruction: Under the h1 heading in the banner, add an img tag (it shows a picture). Set src to ./resources/images/better_than_drake.png, add alt="", and give it id="small-gritty". The src is the path: start here (./), go into resources, then images, then the file.
steps.why: A path tells the page exactly which folders to walk through to find the picture.

checks.say: I can't see Gritty's picture in the banner yet.
The picture's path doesn't point to the images folder yet.
checks.name: src

hints: Add the picture just below the big heading.
After the h1 line, add an img tag with three settings: src (the path to the picture), alt, and id set to small-gritty.

concept.title: Images and relative paths
concept.explain: An img shows a picture; its path says which folders to walk through from this file to find it.

quiz.question: What does ./ at the start of a path mean?
options: Start from the folder this page is in
quiz.explain: ./ means 'start right here', in the same folder as index.html.

steps.title: Look at the plain page
steps.instruction: Watch Brendan open index.html in Chrome. Open your page too: it works but looks plain, because there's no styling yet.
steps.why: Checking often helps you catch mistakes early.
hints: Open your page in the browser preview.
You should see the heading, the picture, the button, the form and one post.
If the picture is missing, check the file name and folders.

steps.title: Add two more posts
steps.instruction: Inside the ul, after the first li, add two more li items built the same way. One says I haven't eaten any other mascots since yesterday. and the other says Burp.
steps.why: Repeating the same pattern is how feeds and lists grow.
steps.expected:
• I haven't eaten any other mascots since yesterday.
  • Burp.

checks.say: Your list should have three posts.
I can't find the Burp post yet.

hints: Copy the shape of your first post twice.
After the first li closes and before the ul closes, add two li items, each with two divs and a span holding the message.

• …
  • …

steps.title: Colour the banner
steps.instruction: Open resources/css/index.css. Write a rule for .banner (the dot means 'things with the class banner'). Inside curly brackets, set background-color (the box's fill colour) to #4D00FF, a purple, and color (the text colour) to white.
steps.why: CSS rules pick things by name and change how they look.

checks.say: I can't see a style rule for the banner yet.
checks.question: Does this CSS have a .banner rule that sets background-color to #4D00FF and color to white?

hints: Write a style rule that targets the banner by its class name.
Start with a dot and the class name, then curly brackets. Inside, set background-color and color, each ending with a semicolon.

concept.title: CSS rules
concept.explain: A CSS rule names what to style, then lists changes like colour inside curly brackets.

steps.title: Space and centre the banner
steps.instruction: Inside the .banner rule, under color, add margin-top: 75px; (empty space above the box) and text-align: center; (puts the text in the middle).
steps.why: Spacing and centring make the banner look neat.

checks.say: The banner still needs space above it and centred text.
checks.question: Does the .banner rule set margin-top to 75px and text-align to center?

hints: Add two more settings to the same banner rule.
Below the color line, add margin-top and text-align, each with a value and a semicolon.

margin-top: …;
text-align: …;

concept.title: Margin and text-align
concept.explain: Margin adds empty space outside a box; text-align decides if text sits left, right or centre.

steps.title: Connect the CSS file
steps.instruction: Back in index.html, at the bottom of the head (after the title), add a link tag with rel="stylesheet" and href="./resources/css/index.css". The link tag connects your styles to the page. Refresh and the banner turns purple!
steps.why: The page can't use your styles until you tell it where the CSS file is.

checks.say: Your page isn't connected to your style file yet.
checks.name: href

checks.say: The banner isn't purple yet. Check the path to your style file.

hints: The page needs to be told where your style file lives.
In the head, right after the title line, add a link tag with rel set to stylesheet and href set to the path of index.css.
<link rel="…" href="./resources/…/…">

concept.title: Linking a stylesheet
concept.explain: The link tag in the head tells the page which CSS file to use for its looks.

quiz.question: Where does the link tag go?
options: At the very end of the body
quiz.explain: Page settings like the stylesheet link belong in the head.

steps.title: Shrink the picture
steps.instruction: In index.css, below the .banner rule, add a rule for #small-gritty (the # means 'the thing with this id'). Set height to 100px and width to 100px. px means pixels, tiny dots on the screen.
steps.why: Big pictures can take over a page, so we set their size.

checks.say: Gritty's picture isn't 100 pixels wide yet.
Gritty's picture isn't 100 pixels tall yet.

hints: Make a new rule for the picture using its id name.
After the banner rule's closing bracket, start with a hash sign and the id, then set height and width.

concept.title: Height and width
concept.explain: Height and width set how tall and how wide something is, often in pixels (px).

steps.title: Give the banner room
steps.instruction: In the .banner rule, under text-align, add padding: 100px 0; Padding is space inside the box, around its contents. The first number is top and bottom, the second is left and right.
steps.why: Padding stops content from feeling squashed against the edges.

checks.say: The banner doesn't have space at the top inside it yet.

hints: Add space inside the banner, above and below the content.
In the banner rule, after the text-align line, add padding with two values.
padding: … …;

concept.title: Padding
concept.explain: Padding is empty space inside a box, between its edge and what's inside.

steps.title: Make the Gritter title huge
steps.instruction: At the bottom of index.css, add a rule for #gritter. Set color to #4D00FF (the same purple) and font-size (how big the letters are) to 100px.
steps.why: A big, bright title makes the section stand out.

checks.say: The Gritter title isn't huge yet.
The Gritter title isn't purple yet.

hints: Write a new rule for the Gritter title using its id.
At the end of the file, use a hash sign and gritter, then set color and font-size.

concept.title: Font size
concept.explain: font-size sets how big the letters are.

steps.title: Make a reusable bold style
steps.instruction: At the bottom of index.css, add a rule for .bold and set font-weight (how thick the letters are) to 900, the thickest. Your paragraph with class bold now looks heavy, and you can reuse this class anywhere.
steps.why: A class can be reused on many things, so one rule styles them all.

checks.say: The bold paragraph isn't extra thick yet.

hints: Write a rule for the class named bold.
At the end of the file, use a dot and bold, then set font-weight inside the brackets.

concept.title: Font weight
concept.explain: font-weight sets how thick letters look; 400 is normal and 900 is the boldest.

quiz.question: What's the difference between a class (.) and an id (#)?
options: A class can be reused; an id is for one thing only
An id can be reused; a class is for one thing only
quiz.explain: Classes are for groups of things, ids name just one.

steps.title: Wrap up
steps.instruction: Watch Brendan sum up: you built a page with HTML, added a picture with a path, linked a CSS file and styled things by class and id.
steps.why: Looking back helps the new ideas stick.
hints: Nothing to type, just enjoy your page.
Try changing a colour in your CSS to see what happens.
Your finished page has a purple banner and a huge Gritter title.
